item.title: IDEA: What Are Thanksgiving Sides That Don’t Need to Go in the Oven?
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
There are millions of recipes on the internet, but you still don’t know what to cook. Tell us about it! Dear Bon Appétit is an advice column where we answer your culinary conundrums with hand-picked recipes and well-seasoned advice. Submit a question here. On Thanksgiving the oven is always precious real estate for the quintessential spread—stuffing, green bean casserole, sweet potatoes, and of course the turkey. In years past, the stress of getting everything in and out of the oven with the right amount of time has been a nuisance that I’d like to avoid this year. Are there any Thanksgiving sides that feel classic but don’t need the oven? —Oven-whelmed If there was a proverbial dartboard of Thanksgiving problems, you have just hit the bullseye. (And as someone who has never hit a real bullseye in her life, I mean this as quite the compliment!) Even if you place oven racks strategically—even if you have one of those fancy double ovens—there’s always a bottleneck of dishes that need to be roasted and baked. The solution is not to plot out an overwrought schedule of when things go in and out, and in and out, but to ruthlessly reduce the number of recipes that require the oven in the first place. With that in mind, I would like to point out that turkey can thrive in other settings. And no, I’m not talking about deep-frying it in your yard, which we all know is a rowdy and risky idea, as proven in Gilmore Girls season three episode nine. You could grill it. You could smoke it. Both delightful. But you asked about sides specifically, so sides are what we will tackle today. Beyond the classics like mashed potatoes, boxed stuffing, and cranberry sauce, here are 10 recipes that do not need an oven at all—and brazenly, boldly get away with it. Green Beans and Mushrooms With Crispy Shallots. The same cozy flavors as a classic green bean casserole—earthy mushrooms, frizzled shallots—but it comes together entirely on the stovetop. Now is the time to branch beyond white button or baby bella; opt for shiitake or oyster, the wonkier the shape the better. Green Beans With Tahini Sbagliato. For something less traditional, from Samin Nosrat’s recent cookbook, this recipe is make-ahead-friendly on multiple fronts. You can blanch the green beans a day ahead and whip up the tahini-miso sauce up to four days ahead. All that’s left on Turkey Day is assembly. Brussels Sprouts Stir-Fry With Cheddar and Golden Raisins. Thinly sliced and swiftly sautéed, brussels sprouts take on a savory char. The cheddar could be swapped out for Gouda, or any aged cheese you love. Likewise, the golden raisins could be replaced with dried cranberries or chopped dates. It’s flexible! Air Fryer Crispy Brussels Sprouts With Honey Butter. Or free up the stove and turn to your trusty air fryer instead. In the concentrated and circulating heat, the sprouts’ outer leaves become crackly like potato chips, craveable enough to go back for thirds. Sweet Potatoes With Tahini Butter. Most sweet potatoes in our archive are roasted, so isn’t it ironic that one of our most popular recipes is steamed. Author Carla Lalli puts it perfectly: “Steaming offers extreme speed and high hydration, which means that whatever you cook will be done quickly and always moist. Sweet potatoes in particular benefit from this treatment, which makes their flesh pudding-like and fluffy.” Glazed Carrots. Li’l retro! These saucy carrots are sweet but not too sweet, thanks to a floral mixture of orange juice and honey, plus a welcome zing from fresh ginger. I could see parsnips swapping in happily here. Parsnip Purée. Speaking of parsnips, from the Barefoot Contessa herself, this is a cousin to mashed potatoes that, in my humble opinion, is a whole lot better. Parsnips have a je ne sais quois, needing no more than butter, salt, and pepper, to shine bright. Adult Mac and Cheese. Despite its title, this dish will be a hit with grown-ups and kids alike. It comes together on the stove with just six ingredients (and that’s including salt!). A few of its rave reviews: “Staple now in my house,” “Super easy and always delicious!” and “Lovelovelove. I’ve made this so many times.” Medium shells catch the sauce like little canoes; or could be a fun moment for radiatori. Kale Salad With Pecan Vinaigrette. Pecans are good for more than pie. Here they turn into a nutty dressing for ruffled kale and perky radishes. Though salad is not the first (or even second) thing one might think of for Thanksgiving, it has become an absolute must on my family’s table. A refreshing reprieve to all the richness. We have more great options here. Instant Pot Collard Greens. On a holiday table, when there’s so much going on, sometimes a simple dish is just the thing. Bacon, greens, onion, chile, done. An Instant Pot is like a Thanksgiving cheat code, freeing up the oven and the stove too. Readers, what sides are you making this year for Thanksgiving? Share menu inspiration in the comments! Questions may be lightly edited for clarity, length, and style.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Herby Sheet-Pan Meatballs With Feta
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
These aren’t your slow-braised, leisurely Sunday-sauce meatballs. They’re let’s-get-this-crew-fed-at-the-end-of-a-busy-workday meatballs. The large amount of breadcrumbs isn’t just a filler; combined with the water, they make the meatballs impossibly tender and springy. You can use any ground meat you’d like; pork, lamb, turkey, or chicken (only dark meat for the poultry, though) all work well. Roasting the meatballs in the oven instead of frying them on the stovetop reduces the active cook time and makes cleanup simple. Need to make a substitution? - Step 1Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 425°. Using a sturdy wooden spoon, vigorously mix 2 large eggs, zest of 1 lemon, 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, 1 cup panko, ½ cup finely chopped dill and/or parsley, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 2 tsp. dried oregano, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, 1 tsp. ground cumin, and ½ cup water in a large bowl until nearly a smooth paste. Add 1 lb. ground beef and mix vigorously until well combined and mixture is slightly tacky. Oil your hands; divide mixture into 16 portions and roll into balls. Arrange on a large rimmed baking sheet. Step 2Toss 1 large red onion, cut through root end into 2"-thick wedges, 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, a large pinch of salt, and a large pinch of pepper in a small bowl. Arrange in a single layer around meatballs. Bake meatballs and onions until meatballs are deeply browned underneath and an instant-read thermometer inserted into centers registers 160°, 25–30 minutes. Let cool slightly. Step 3To serve, generously top with sliced cucumbers, crumbled feta, and more dill and/or parsley if desired. Serve with country-style bread and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: The Cheapest Ways to Get Around the British Countryside
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
Rolling hills, stone villages and quiet country lanes are a big part of Britain's charm, but getting around isn't always easy or cheap. The nearest station might be miles from the village, the bus may run twice a day, and a taxi across the county can cost more than the day out itself. Whether you're exploring the Cotswolds, visiting family in rural Wales, or commuting from a village to the nearest market town, how you choose to travel can make a surprising difference to what you spend. The good news is that there are plenty of affordable options, and the cheapest approach usually combines several of them. Here's how to work out what suits you and make each option go further. Before comparing fares, think about how you travel. How often do you need to go somewhere? How far? Will you share some journeys with others? In the countryside, it's easy to assume a car is the only answer, but if you only need transport occasionally, owning one may cost far more than alternatives. If you rely on a car most days, it pays to look beyond the sticker price. Fuel, insurance, servicing, and repairs all add up, so comparing these costs alongside affordable used car leasing options can help you see what you'd really pay each month. Once you know your true transport needs, it becomes easier to choose the cheapest way to meet them. In rural areas, a little planning saves money. Some bus routes run only a few times a day, and many don't run on Sundays or bank holidays. Check timetables before you set off using journey-planning apps or your council's website, which often lists community buses and on-demand services. If you're combining walking, cycling, buses and trains, mapping your route in advance is the best way to avoid an expensive last-minute taxi. Buses are often the cheapest way to get between villages and towns. Fare caps in many parts of England have made short and medium journeys especially good value, and Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland all have concessionary schemes. Depending on your age or circumstances, you may even qualify for free or discounted travel, with schemes for young people, students and older passengers. The catch is frequency. Because rural services can be limited, treat the timetable as the starting point of your plan, not an afterthought. If you're flexible, buses work well for shopping trips, medical appointments, days out and getting to the nearest railway station. If you're making several journeys in one area, a return or day ticket can reduce the cost further. For longer journeys, trains can be excellent value if you book wisely. Advance tickets and off-peak fares can cut the price significantly, and a railcard usually pays for itself after just a few trips a year. You can compare the options for young people, families, couples, older people and disabled passengers on the official Railcard website. The challenge is that many countryside destinations don't have a station. The smart approach is to use the train for the long, expensive part of the journey, then switch to a bus, bike or lift for the last few miles. Taking a train to a nearby town and finishing by local bus is often much cheaper than a taxi all the way from your door. Once you've covered the cost of a bike, helmet, lights and a basic repair kit, cycling costs little to run. Britain is crisscrossed with quiet lanes, bridleways and signed cycle routes, making it ideal for short trips to the shop, station, school or work. In hilly areas or for longer commutes, an electric bike can make cycling more realistic. E-bikes cost more upfront but are usually cheaper than running a car. If you're not sure whether one is right for you, look for hire schemes, local trials or a second-hand bike from a reputable seller. Whatever you ride, think about road safety, visibility and a secure place to store it. Walking is free, good for you and often quicker than you think. In villages and small towns, many trips under a mile take less time on foot than arranging a lift or waiting for a bus. Sturdy shoes, a waterproof jacket and a torch for darker evenings make walking practical year-round. Walking pairs well with public transport for days out. Take a bus or train to one village, walk to the next, then catch a ride home. You'll avoid parking charges and see more of the countryside along the way, from Cornish coastal paths to the fells of the Lake District, two of the best places to explore on foot in the UK. When a car trip is unavoidable, sharing it is one of the simplest ways to save. If neighbors, colleagues or friends head the same way, splitting fuel and parking costs benefits everyone. It works well for commuting, school runs, weekly shopping trips and events. As well as informal arrangements between neighbors, there are lift-sharing platforms, workplace schemes and community groups that help people coordinate journeys. Whichever you use, agree on costs and timings upfront to avoid misunderstandings. Sharing one or two trips a week can be enough for some households to manage without a second car. For people who find ordinary buses hard to use, community transport can be a lifeline. Many rural areas offer dial-a-ride minibusses, volunteer driver schemes, and community car services, which are usually much cheaper than taxis and especially valuable for older residents, disabled passengers, and anyone without a car. Eligibility varies. Some services are open to anyone living where public transport is limited, while others focus on medical appointments or essential shopping. Check with your local council, parish council or community transport provider, and expect to book in advance. The cheapest way to get around the UK countryside is rarely just one option. For most people, it's a mix: buses for trips into town, a bike for local errands, the train for longer journeys, walking wherever it's practical, and a shared lift when it's needed. With a bit of planning and the right combination, countryside travel can be far more affordable than it first appears. This story was published in partnership with Hippo Leasing.
